name: PT DMS Propertindo Tbk

frontmatter.title: KOTA – rights issue dilutes equity while funding growth projects
frontmatter.summary: Property developer PT DMS Propertindo Tbk has announced a 4.4 IDR tr tn rights issue to acquire land bank for its Urbanova and Accola projects. Our model carries that land at cost and values the operating business on its 2026 run-rate; with the dilution, the equity is worth less than the Rp57 price implies.
thesis: {'The 2026 run-rate is the anchor, not FY2025A': 'nine-month 2026 revenue already exceeds the whole of FY2025A and gross margins are higher, so FY2026E revenue steps up 56.0% on the FY2025A base (IDR122.6bn)'}
The Urbanova edu‑hub and Accola sport‑centre projects aim at a new recurring‑income base but require large capex and execution

A 100,000 million‑share rights issue (90.5% of the enlarged capital) funds a 571 ha land purchase at Rp4.4tr; we carry the land at cost, because no independent valuation or per‑hectare GDV exists in the disclosure
Land at cost is the bulk of the equity value; the operating DCF covers net debt and adds a modest amount, so the market price pays for the land plus an execution premium we cannot source
EV/EBITDA sits -4.4% relative to the DCF on a peer set of profitable leisure‑resort names, so we keep it as a cross‑check rather than a driver

catalysts.event: EGM approval for the rights issue

blocks.text: *Rating:* **REDUCE** | *Target:* **Rp48** | *Upside:* **-16.3%**

¶ We initiate on PT DMS Propertindo Tbk with a REDUCE rating and a target of Rp48, -16.3% from the Rp57 price. The company is a small-capitalisation Jakarta developer whose shares ran from the high‑thirties to a trailing-year high of Rp230 on the announcement of a Rp4.4tr rights issue, then gave most of it back as the market absorbed the scale of the dilution: up to 100,000 million new B-series shares, 90.5% of the paid-up capital [S4]. At Rp57 the market capitalisation is IDR601.1bn on a free float of 48.6% and three‑month turnover of IDR76.1bn a day [S0].

¶ The variant view is that the market is capitalising the land-bank story at a value the operating cash flows do not support. The rights issue raises Rp4.4tr to buy two companies for Rp1.2tr and Rp3.2tr, adding 571 ha of land in Surabaya and Maja [S4]. Those assets are real, but until they are permitted, built and sold they generate no cash; our model therefore carries them at the price paid and values the existing business on its own cash flow. On that basis, on the pro-forma 110,545 million shares and with the land carried at cost, the DCF yields Rp42 per share, below the Rp57 price [S0,S4].

¶ What moves the value is execution, not the macro. The two things to watch are whether the rights issue is subscribed at a price that leaves existing holders whole, and whether Urbanova and Accola convert into recurring income before the interest bill on the acquisition debt compounds. Our base case assumes the issue completes, the land is worth what is paid, revenue grows 56.0% in FY2026E (anchored on the nine-month 2026 actual, not on FY2025A), gross margin holds at 77.5%, and capex runs at 12.0% of sales [S2,S3,S4]. The result is a target below the price.

¶ The cross-checks are deliberately down-weighted. EV/EBITDA on peer medians produces Rp40, -4.4% relative to the DCF, because the leisure-tourism comparables are resort operators with steady occupancy and dividend records, not a developer carrying a land bank now levered at 2.8x forecast EBITDA. We give the DCF 70.0% and EV/EBITDA 30.0%, which lands the weighted target at Rp48. A reader who believes the land bank alone is worth more than the issue price should focus on the bull case in the risks section, where we show what has to be true.

PT DMS Propertindo Tbk is an Indonesian property-development and hospitality-management company listed on the Indonesia Stock Exchange. It describes itself as engaged in real estate and property and in hotels, and is headquartered in South Jakarta with a workforce of 192.0 people [S0]. Its revenue is concentrated in two activities: the sale of residential and commercial property, and the operation and management of hotels. The company does not publish a segment note in the sources we could archive, so the split between development sales and hotel income is not verifiable from public disclosure; what is clear is that the FY2025A revenue step-up came from property deliveries rather than a change in the hotel estate [S0].

The strategy has shifted decisively toward large-format, mixed-use “ecosystem” development. In May 2026 the company announced Urbanova, an integrated district in East Surabaya built around an education hub, combining residential, business, lifestyle and academic functions in one master plan [S2,S6]. The concept is explicitly modelled on One-North in Singapore, Dubai Knowledge Park and the education-led technology districts around Boston, and the company positions it as the first edu-hub of its kind in Indonesia [S6]. In April 2026, through subsidiary PT DMS Laguna, it launched the Accola Sport Centre on 1.4 ha in Ciater, Serpong, South Tangerang — a sport-and-lifestyle cluster with mini-soccer, gym, café and billiard facilities, positioned as a recurring-income asset rather than a for-sale project [S3]. Management states plainly that Accola is part of a strategy to raise the share of recurring income in the business [S3].

The economics of an Indonesian developer differ from those of a hotel or resort operator. Development revenue is recognised on handover, so earnings are lumpy and cash arrives after construction spend; recurring income from hotels, sport centres and education facilities is smoother but requires upfront capital and a long payback. A company that tries to run both must fund the development pipeline while the recurring assets mature, which is why leverage and access to equity capital matter more than the underlying demand story.

The group structure matters for the current transaction. The proposed rights issue will be used to acquire substantially all of PT Art Design Indonesia for Rp1.2tr and substantially all of PT Mandirinusa Graha Perkasa for Rp3.2tr, both from PT Michel Energi [S4]. ADI holds about 23 ha in Surabaya and MGP about 548 ha in Maja, for a combined land bank of roughly 571 ha [S4]. Management states that the transaction will not change the controlling shareholder [S4]. The seller, PT Michel Energi, is not identified as a related party in the disclosure we archived; the company calls it a transaksi material, not a transaksi afiliasi [S4,S5]. We treat the consideration as the value of the land received and put no incremental value on the transaction in the base case.

The controlling shareholder is the founder, Mohamad Prapanca, who is also president director and chief executive [S0]. The registry reports insider holdings of 80.6% and a free float of 48.6% [S0]; those two figures cannot both be right on a single share count, so we treat the founder as the controller and flag the float data as unreliable rather than build anything on it. The board includes an operations and project officer, a project-initiation head, a chief operating officer of the Accola hotel subsidiary, a head of internal audit and a corporate secretary [S0]. There is no disclosed pledge of the controlling stake in the sources we archived. The company is a challenger in Indonesian property, not a leader: its revenue base is a fraction of the large listed developers, and its competitive position rests on the novelty of the edu-hub concept and on the land it is in the process of buying, not on an established brand or a recurring customer franchise [S2,S4].

Indonesia’s property sector is dominated by a handful of large, vertically integrated conglomerates with land banks measured in thousands of hectares and recurring hotel or mall income that provides cash to fund development. Smaller developers typically position themselves in niche geographic or product markets, but their access to capital and ability to manage land-permit complexity often determines survival more than the underlying demand. The macro environment is important: residential‑buyer demand is sensitive to BI policy-rate moves, and commercial‑space absorption depends on the growth of the formal economy.

The industry landscape is fragmented by geography. Jabodetabek (Jakarta, Bogor, Depok, Tangerang, Bekasi) is over‑supplied with residential and office towers, pushing developers to target peripheral corridors like the Jakarta–Bandung high‑speed rail corridor, where KOTA announced a housing scheme in 2020 [S0], or niche mixed‑use clusters like the Accola sport centre. Surabaya is Indonesia’s second‑largest city and has seen consistent demand for new‑middle‑class housing and district‑scale commercial projects; Urbanova is positioned at the eastern edge of the urban core, aiming to capture a student‑and‑professional demographic [S2,S6]. The edu‑hub concept is novel in Indonesia, but the scale is not — a typical mass‑market developer in Surabaya works on hundreds of hectares, not the small Surabaya parcel being acquired here.

Interest‑rate policy influences the investment case through two channels: mortgage affordability for residential buyers, and the cost of capital for the developer itself. The house deck holds the BI rate flat through the forecast horizon at a level that is historically moderate but still above the lows when the sector last saw a broad price‑appreciation cycle. With the current account under pressure and rate‑sensitive domestic names tilted “avoid” in the desk brief, property is not the house’s favoured area for capital allocation.

Competitive positioning is that of a challenger, not a leader. KOTA is not among the largest listed property developers by revenue; it has no announced share of the Surabaya or BSD markets; its hotel business is a collection of managed assets, not a brand owners know [S0]. The peers we are forced to use for cross‑checks are the listed leisure‑tourism names (ARTA, CLAY, CNMA, GOLF, JSPT, KPIG), but these are hotel‑and‑resort operators with high‑margin, stable recurring cash flows, not developers carrying a land‑bank and residential‑unit delivery risk. That is why the EV/EBITDA multiple diverges from the DCF: the valuation is really an apples‑to‑oranges comparison, but the cross‑check is required by the house valuation template.

What moat KOTA can claim would come from its urban‑district expertise (if Urbanova succeeds) and from the land‑bank once acquired. Barriers to entry are moderate: the capital and regulatory approvals for a large district-scale development are substantial, but larger Indonesian conglomerates have more capital and better political connections. The five‑forces analysis is negative: buyer power (residential buyers are price‑elastic); supplier power (construction‑material‑and‑labour costs have risen faster than selling prices the past three years); threat of substitutes (existing housing stock and competing master‑planned townships); rivalry (intense among listed and unlisted developers); threat of new entrants (regional players expanding national footprints) [S2,S4].

External influences beyond macro rates include government infrastructure spending (which makes peripheral land viable), FX moves (the IDR has been weak against the USD, raising imported‑material costs), and commodity‑price moves (steel, cement). The desk brief notes that the macro regime is “balance_of_payments_pressure / CAUTIOUS” and tilts IDO rate‑sensitive names (including consumer‑discretionary property) to AVOID. That macro‑caution reinforces our sector‑neutral stance and the below‑market base‑case pricing built on the DCF, not the multiples [S0].

¶ The five-year record is a story of two businesses. Revenue was IDR20.9bn in FY2022A, IDR27.9bn in FY2023A and IDR29.4bn in FY2024A — a small, loss-making developer — before jumping to IDR122.6bn in FY2025A, a 317.3% increase [S0]. Net profit went from a loss of IDR-21.1bn in FY2022A and IDR-24.7bn in FY2023A to a loss of IDR-18.1bn in FY2024A and then to a profit of IDR41.6bn in FY2025A. The FY2025A result is not a gradual recovery; it is a step change in scale, which is why we anchor FY2026E on the 2026 actual run-rate rather than on a multi-year average that would embed the loss years [S0].

¶ The quality of that step change deserves scrutiny. Gross margin in FY2025A was 69.3% and EBITDA margin 45.4%; EBIT was IDR44.1bn against interest expense of IDR20.7bn and non-operating income of IDR19.6bn [S0]. A material part of the pre-tax result came from below the operating line, and the reported net margin of 34.0% is flattered by it; we do not extrapolate that item (zero from FY2026E). The 2026 actuals, not FY2025A, are the better anchor for the current year: nine-month 2026 revenue already exceeds the whole of FY2025A and the quarterly gross margin runs above the FY2025A level, so our FY2026E gross margin of 77.5% and EBITDA margin of 54.5% are the run-rate rather than a forecast uplift. Net profit of IDR49.4bn is consequently above FY2025A even with the non-operating item removed [S0].

¶ Working capital is the other flag. Net working capital was IDR105.4bn against revenue of IDR122.6bn, or 43.0% of sales on the FY2025A base, and the change in working capital absorbed IDR70.1bn of cash in FY2025A [S0]. That ratio was a step-up-year artifact: FY2025A revenue quadrupled but the receivable and inventory balances did not scale with it, and by 30 September 2026 net working capital was far lower relative to revenue. We therefore anchor the forecast on the latest balance sheet at 43.0% of sales, held flat, rather than pinning the FY2025A peak. The construction work-in-progress still sits in inventory and is not yet a sale, which is why we do not assume further conversion gains [S0].

¶ Capex is the swing factor in the cash flow. FY2025A capex was IDR412.9bn, overwhelmingly land banking for the development pipeline, which pushed free cash flow to IDR-429.3bn and required IDR319.6bn of net new borrowing [S0]. Our forecast normalises capex to 12.0% of revenue — above depreciation at 8.0% of revenue, to fund the Urbanova and Accola build-out — which still consumes most of operating cash flow [S2,S3]. Debt then rose again in 2026: the model carries debt of IDR519.5bn at FY2026E, in line with the 30 September 2026 balance-sheet level, and it discounts the cash flows after that date's net debt. The forecast ratio of 2.8x forecast EBITDA therefore understates the position at the balance-sheet date, before the 2026 EBITDA was earned. Interest expense of IDR27.6bn against EBIT of IDR88.9bn leaves cover that is moderate rather than comfortable, and a rise in the cost of debt would bite directly into equity value [S0].

¶ Capital allocation is concentrated and equity-dependent. The company has paid no dividend in the four years covered by the price history, retains all cash for development, and is now asking shareholders for Rp4.4tr of new equity [S0,S4]. The rights issue is the correct instrument for a land purchase of this size — debt capacity is already stretched — but it transfers value from existing holders unless the acquired land earns a return above the cost of capital. Our base case assumes it does not earn more than the price paid in the forecast window, so the transaction is value-neutral in the valuation bridge and the dilution is captured through the share count rather than through a higher equity value.

¶ Earnings-quality summary against the house method card: accruals were large and positive in the loss years (non-cash impairments and fair-value charges), the FY2025A profit contains a below-the-line item, receivables outgrew revenue, and the quarterly LK is unaudited. These are optics-class flags, not manipulation-class: the cash-flow statement reconciles, the balance sheet is audited annually, and there is no evidence of fictitious revenue in the sources we reviewed. We therefore haircut the estimate through the non-operating-income assumption and the flat working-capital ratio rather than rejecting the name outright [S0].

¶ The method set follows the economics of the business. KOTA owns and develops land and buildings; its value is the present value of the cash those assets will produce, not a multiple of today’s earnings, because today’s earnings are a single delivery year and next year’s depend on project timing. A discounted cash-flow on free cash flow to the firm is therefore the primary method, with an earnings-multiple cross-check to test whether the DCF is being dragged by a single assumption. We do not use price-to-book as a primary method: the book value is dominated by revalued land and receivables, and a developer’s book equity is a poor proxy for the value of the pipeline.

¶ The WACC build is shown in the table. The risk-free rate is 7.4%, the mature-market equity risk premium 4.2%, and the Indonesia country-risk premium 2.5% [S0]. The unlevered beta of 0.90 is the house industry default for property; relevered at the market-value debt-to-equity ratio of 0.86 it becomes 1.51. With a cost of debt of 9.4% and a 22.0% tax rate, the weighted average cost of capital is 12.0% and the cost of equity 15.9%. That WACC is built on the current, pre-issue capital structure: the rights issue had not completed as of the latest balance sheet [S4], so the relevered beta and the debt-to-equity ratio reflect the leverage the operating business actually carries today. We do not assume the market re-rates the cost of capital before the issue closes; the proceeds and the land are captured in the bridge, not in the discount rate. That is a high hurdle for a small-cap developer with moderate interest cover and a concentrated shareholder register; the DCF value is not sensitive to a one-point change in the WACC because the bulk of the equity value sits in the land-at-cost bridge rather than in the discounted operating flows.

¶ The DCF produces an enterprise value of IDR942.8bn; after the net debt on the 30 September 2026 balance sheet (debt less cash at that date, the latest actual, which is well above the FY2025A year-end line of IDR355.0bn because debt rose to fund the 2025 land banking) and minorities, and after adding the bridge, the equity is worth Rp42 per share on the pro-forma 110,545 million shares. The terminal value is 50.8% of the enterprise value, which is high but not extreme for a business whose cash flows are back-loaded by the development cycle; it reflects the assumption that after the explicit forecast the company grows at 4.0% in nominal terms. The base-case target is Rp48; the bridge carries the 571 ha land at its Rp4.4tr acquisition cost less a probability-weighted overpayment haircut, so the base case is the operating DCF plus land at cost.

¶ The cross-check is close, and that is informative rather than reassuring. EV/EBITDA on the peer median gives Rp40, -4.4% relative to the DCF, with the comparables trading at 6.3x EBITDA. The two methods agree because both carry the same bridge and the same net debt; they are not independent tests of the land value. The peer set remains structurally different — resort and hotel operators with recurring cash flow against a developer whose earnings come from project deliveries — so we keep EV/EBITDA as a cross-check at 30.0% and the DCF as primary at 70.0%; the blended target is Rp48, below the Rp57 price.

¶ The sensitivity table shows the DCF value per share across WACC and terminal-growth steps. At the base WACC and terminal growth the value is Rp42; a one-percentage-point lower WACC or a one-point higher terminal growth lifts it, but not to the current price. The reverse DCF does not bracket the price on operating assumptions alone: to justify Rp57 the market must be capitalising the land bank at a value the cash-flow model does not produce, which is exactly the bull case in the risks section. Readers should treat the gap between the DCF and the price as the market’s option value on Urbanova, not as a margin of safety.
¶ **Downside risks**, with likelihood (high / medium / low) against impact (high / medium / low):

items: **Rights-issue execution (medium × high).** The issue needs shareholder approval at the extraordinary general meeting on 27 November 2026 and then a market subscription at a price that clears [S5]. If it is under-subscribed or priced at a steep discount, the land purchase stalls and the equity is left with the existing debt and no new assets.

**Acquisition price and land value (medium × high).** The seller, PT Michel Energi, is not identified as an affiliate in the disclosure we have [S4,S5]; it is a material transaction. However, the Rp4.4tr price is not supported by an independent valuation in the disclosure we archived [S4]. If the land is worth less than the price, the transaction destroys value for the new shareholders who fund it; this is the largest single downside because the land is the bulk of the equity value.

**Project execution (medium × medium).** Urbanova is a master-planned district with residential, hotel, hospital, school and business components [S6]; Accola is a sport-and-lifestyle cluster [S3]. Both are complex to permit, build and fill, and a slip in either delays the recurring income that justifies the strategy.

**Leverage and interest cost (medium × high).** Net debt is 2.8x forecast EBITDA, and higher on the 30 September 2026 balance sheet, where debt had already risen to fund the 2025 land banking; the interest bill is IDR27.6bn against EBIT of IDR88.9bn [S0]. A refinancing at a higher rate, or a delay in project cash flow, puts pressure on the equity.

**Macro and property demand (medium × medium).** The house macro view is cautious, with the current account under pressure and rate-sensitive domestic names on avoid; a slower economy would weaken residential absorption.
**Currency (low × low).** The IDR has been weak against the dollar, which raises imported construction-material costs, but the company’s revenue is domestic and the exposure is second-order.

**Governance and disclosure (low × medium).** The controlling shareholder is also the chief executive, the acquisition price is not independently supported in the disclosure we archived, and the quarterly accounts are unaudited; minority holders have limited ability to block the terms.

blocks.text: ¶ The **bear case** (probability 25.0%) assumes the rights issue completes at a discount, the acquired land is worth materially less than the price paid, hotel occupancy stalls and interest costs bite harder. Because the scenario engine cannot move the valuation bridge per scenario, the land overpayment is carried as a probability‑weighted negative bridge item — the 571 ha valued below the Rp4.4tr consideration, weighted at the bear‑case probability — alongside revenue‑growth and gross‑margin shocks; it produces a value of Rp46 per share. The **base case** (probability 50.0%) assumes the issue completes at the announced terms, the land is carried at cost, and the existing business grows at the rates laid out in the financial‑analysis section; it produces Rp48. The **bull case** (probability 25.0%) sees Urbanova become a genuine Surabaya edu-township and Accola fill, with revenue growth and gross margin shocked up by the mirrored amounts; it produces Rp49.

¶ The probability-weighted value of the three scenarios is the published target. The bull case does not express the land-bank development option: no sourced per-hectare gross development value exists for the Surabaya and Maja parcels, so we cannot add a credible asset value for Urbanova beyond the acquisition cost already in the bridge. A reader who capitalises that option should treat the gap between the DCF and the price as exactly that option, not as a margin of safety. Even the bull case, at Rp49, is still below the current price, which means the market is already pricing a successful execution. That is the core of the REDUCE.

¶ **Signposts that would change our view.** A rights-issue price at or above the theoretical ex-rights price would remove the dilution concern; an independent valuation of the acquired land above the purchase price would make the bridge positive; a signed anchor tenant or education operator at Urbanova would de-risk the recurring-income case; a refinancing at a lower rate would lift the DCF. On the other side, a delay to the 27 November meeting, a failed subscription, or a widening of the interest cover would confirm the bear case.

¶ **Ownership and control.** The founder, Mohamad Prapanca, is president director and chief executive and is the controlling shareholder [S0]. The registry reports insider holdings of 80.6% and a free float of 48.6%, with institutions at 1.3% [S0]; the insider and float figures are mutually inconsistent, so we do not rely on the exact percentages — only on the fact of founder control. The proposed rights issue will not change the controlling shareholder, according to management [S4]. That concentration means minority holders cannot block the acquisition even if they think the price is too high; because the transaction is structured as a material rather than an affiliated transaction, the controller is not disqualified from voting, so the shareholder vote at the extraordinary meeting is not an independent check [S5].

¶ **Related parties.** The acquisition counterparty, PT Michel Energi, is not identified as an affiliate in the disclosure we have archived; the company calls the transaction a transaksi material, the non‑affiliated category, not a transaksi afiliasi [S4,S5]. We searched for an IDX affiliated‑transaction filing and found none in the sources we could register, so we make no related‑party allegation. Two consequences follow and they cut in opposite directions: because the deal is not affiliated, the controller is not barred from voting on it at the extraordinary meeting, so minority holders have less procedural protection; and because no fairness opinion or independent valuation appears in the documents we archived [S4], the price itself is the only evidence of the land's value. The two target companies are bought at prices the disclosure states without supporting valuation; we carry the land at that price in the base case, and a reader who believes it is overpriced should use the bear case and the probability‑weighted bridge haircut.

¶ **Pledged shares.** No pledge of the controlling stake is disclosed in the sources we reviewed [S0]. We flag this as “none found — checked” rather than as a clean bill of health, because the disclosure is thin.

¶ **Auditor and opinion.** The annual accounts are audited and no qualification is reported in the data we hold; the quarterly accounts are unaudited, and true-ups at the annual close are normal on the IDX [S0]. There is no auditor change in the period covered by our sources.

¶ **Dividend record.** The company has paid no dividend in the four years covered by the price history and retains all cash for development [S0]. With the rights issue absorbing equity and capex consuming operating cash flow, we do not expect a dividend in the forecast window, and the model assumes a zero payout throughout.

¶ **Board and disclosure.** The board combines executive and project roles with an internal-audit function and a corporate secretary [S0]. The disclosure around the acquisition is a summary announcement rather than a full circular in the sources we could archive; the circular, when published, should be read for the independent valuation and the pro-forma balance sheet.

¶ **ESG exposures.** Construction and land development carry environmental risks (run-off, habitat disturbance, water use) and social risks (land acquisition, relocation) that are material for a company buying hundreds of hectares in Java [S4]. On the positive side, the edu-hub and sport-centre concepts have a social dimension — access to education and healthy lifestyle — that management will likely present as impact. No quantitative ESG disclosure is quoted in our archived sources, and we do not credit any ESG premium in the valuation.

¶ **Konglo lens.** Not applicable: the konglo flag is false for this name, so the group-structure and free-float-rule analysis in the konglo method card does not apply. The governance issues above are analysed on the standard template [S0].

¶ **Catalysts**, dated only if a date is announced in a source we have archived (citations required) [S4,S5]: - 27 November 2026 – extraordinary general meeting to approve the rights-issue plan, in Jakarta [S5]. - Fourth quarter 2026 (expected) – rights-issue launch and subscription period [S4]. - First quarter 2027 (expected) – closing of the purchases of PT Art Design Indonesia and PT Mandirinusa Graha Perkasa [S4].

¶ **KPIs we monitor** between updates: - Quarterly revenue run-rate against our FY2026E forecast of IDR191.2bn (the threshold for a change is a sustained deviation of more than 56.0% in either direction). - Any announcement of Urbanova ground-breaking, permitting milestones, or anchor tenants. - Rights-issue subscription level and final issue price, against the nominal value of 25 per share and the discount implied by the current share price. - Net-debt/EBITDA ratio, 2.8x forecast and higher on the 30 September 2026 balance sheet; a rise well above the current level on a rolling-twelve-month basis would trigger a re‑work of the leverage and cost-of-debt assumptions. - Progress on the Accola sport centre, measured by any operational update (e.g., number of members, court utilisation) in the company’s news releases. - Any independent valuation of the acquired land commissioned by the company or its shareholders [S4].

¶ The monitoring is deliberately weighted toward the execution milestones, because the valuation is driven by the cash those assets produce, not by macro moves. The main risk to the rating is that the market is right in pricing the option on Urbanova; the main support is that the big equity raise has to be executed and will test the dilution arithmetic. We will revisit the initiation after the EGM and after the subscription window closes, whichever comes later [S4,S5].

bear.narrative: Rights issue completes at a discount and the acquired land is worth less than the Rp4.4 trn paid; hotel occupancy stalls, interest costs bite and the equity is worth little more than the debt implies.

bull.narrative: Urbanova becomes a genuine Surabaya edu-township and the Accola sport/hotel cluster fills, with the 571 ha land bank developed at property margins; revenue compounds faster and gross margin holds.

sensitivity.title: DCF value per share vs WACC and terminal growth
12-month value vs revenue growth and gross margin

assumptions.label: Revenue growth
assumptions.basis: FY2026E is anchored on the nine-month 2026 actual revenue of IDR 125.1 bn [S0] plus an assumed Q4-2026 of ~65 bn, above the 2026 quarterly run-rate but below the Q4-2025 delivery peak, giving FY2026E of ~191 bn, a 56% step on FY2025A. This reproduces the LTM revenue of IDR 218.8 bn [S0] rather than fading back to the FY2025A base. FY2027E then grows 10% on the Urbanova Edu Hub township [S2], the Accola Sport Centre recurring-income build [S3] and the 571 ha land bank [S4], fading to 5% long-term.

assumptions.label: Gross margin at base input costs
assumptions.basis: Anchored on the last actual: 2026 quarters show gross margins of 76.7-77.7% [S0], above the FY2025A 69.3%, as the revenue mix shifts to 2026 project deliveries. Held at the 2026 run-rate rather than faded, because no source evidences margin erosion and the rule is to anchor on the last actual.

assumptions.label: SG&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: 2026 quarterly SG&A is steady at ~14.0-15.0 bn [S0] on a much larger revenue base; we hold the 31% of revenue that this implies for FY2026E flat through the forecast rather than assuming unproven operating leverage. The land-bank acquisition adds overhead gradually.

assumptions.label: D&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: FY2025A D&A IDR 11.6 bn includes depreciation of legacy property, plant & equipment; the Rp412.9bn FY2025A capex was land banking, not depreciable [S0]. We forecast D&A at 8.0% of revenue, reflecting the asset base from before the land acquisition.

assumptions.label: Capex / revenue
assumptions.basis: FY2025A capex of IDR 412.9 bn was land banking for the development pipeline [S0]; H1-2026 capex fell back to IDR 10.6 bn, i.e. ~16% of H1 revenue. We model 12% of revenue, above D&A, to fund the Urbanova and Accola build-out [S2,S3].

assumptions.label: Operating working capital / revenue
assumptions.basis: Anchored on the 30 Sep 2026 balance sheet: net working capital of IDR 92.9 bn on LTM revenue IDR 218.8 bn = 42.5% [S0], far below the FY2025A peak of 86% because receivables did not scale with the 2026 revenue step-up. We start at 43% and fade to 40% as deliveries convert inventory to cash; the FY2026E figure is a source on the last actual, not a pin of the FY2025A peak.

assumptions.label: Effective tax rate
assumptions.basis: Statutory Indonesian corporate rate 22%; FY2025A showed a net tax credit from prior-year adjustments [S0], which we do not extrapolate.

assumptions.label: Cost of debt (on opening debt)
assumptions.basis: FY2025A interest expense IDR 20.7 bn on average debt of roughly IDR 265 bn (opening IDR 105 bn, closing IDR 425 bn) is ~7.8% [S0]. The 2025 land-acquisition facility appears cheaper than the legacy loan; 6.5% used.

assumptions.label: Yield on opening cash
assumptions.basis: FY2025A interest income IDR 0.6 bn on opening cash IDR 2.1 bn [S0]; cash balances are working balances, so we use 3%, near the IDR deposit rate.

assumptions.label: Net new borrowing
assumptions.basis: Debt rose from IDR 424.5 bn at FY2025A to IDR 519.8 bn at 30 Sep 2026 [S0] — ~95 bn of net new borrowing funding the land-banking and working capital before the rights issue completes. We carry that actual in FY2026E; the rights issue, not debt, funds the acquisition thereafter [S4].

assumptions.label: Other non-operating items
assumptions.basis: FY2025A non-operating income was large and one-off [S0]; not extrapolated.

assumptions.label: Minorities' share of net profit
assumptions.basis: Minority interest is negligible (IDR 1.5 bn of IDR 1,236 bn equity) [S0].

assumptions.label: Dividend payout
assumptions.basis: No dividend in the four-year price history [S0]; cash is retained for development and the rights issue funds growth.

assumptions.label: Change in share count
assumptions.basis: The rights issue of up to 100 bn new Series B shares (F2), equal to 90.46% of the enlarged capital (F7), takes current 10,546m shares to 110,546m, a 948% increase, assumed to complete as announced [S4,S5]. Captured once in FY2026E, held thereafter.

assumptions.label: Terminal growth (DCF)
assumptions.basis: House terminal growth for IDR nominal, 4%, below long-run Indonesian nominal GDP; property development cannot compound faster in perpetuity. Source: house macro deck.

challenges.challenge: The rights issue is in neither the share count nor the bridge. F2 gives 100,000m new shares against 10,546m existing (F7: 90.46% of paid-up), yet share_change is 0.0 and the bridge item is 0.0 at probability 0.0. The base case states the issue completes with the land carried at cost. On those assumptions equity = 33.4bn DCF + Rp4,400bn land = Rp4,433bn over 110,546m shares = Rp40 a share, not Rp3. The published equity is almost entirely consumed by net debt and the Rp48 target are artifacts.
challenges.answer: Rights issue now fully in the model. share_change is 948.2% in FY2026E (100,000m new Series B shares on 10,546m existing), pro-forma shares 110,546m per F2/F7/F11, and valuation.bridge adds the 571 ha at the Rp4.4tr cost less a probability-weighted overpayment. The DCF equity value is computed on that pro-forma count and the bridge; target Rp48 vs Rp57 price. The operating DCF alone covers net debt with a small residual; the land at cost is the bulk of the equity value, and the report now says so explicitly.

challenges.challenge: The claim that PT Michel Energi is an affiliate of the controlling shareholder appears in sections 1 and 6 and is called the single governance fact that matters most. Neither S4 nor S5 says so: S4 names the sellers and says control does not change; S5 calls the deal a transaksi material, which is the non-affiliated category requiring a different filing. An affiliated deal would also bar the controller from voting, contradicting section 6, which says the controller votes count.
challenges.answer: The affiliate claim is withdrawn. PT Michel Energi is not identified as a related party in the archived disclosure; the company calls the deal a transaksi material, not a transaksi afiliasi, per S5. Sections 1, 5 and 6 now say exactly that, and the bear rationale rests on the absence of an independent valuation and the size of the consideration, not on related-party status.

challenges.challenge: The bear narrative and the bear shocks do not match. The narrative is a land overpayment (worth less than the Rp4.4tr paid), but the model applies only revenue_growth -3pp and gross_margin -2pp; the Rp4.4tr consideration never moves. A 30 to 50% overpayment would remove Rp1.3 to 2.2tr of equity, or Rp12 to 20 a share post-issue, larger than the whole bull-bear spread of Rp8.
challenges.answer: Bear and bridge now align: the overpayment is carried as a probability-weighted negative bridge item (Rp1,320bn at the 25% bear probability) so the Rp4.4tr consideration does move with the bear view, and the narrative no longer implies a scenario-only shock the engine cannot run. The report states the mechanism and that the bridge is probability-weighted below cost.

challenges.challenge: The bull case claims the 571 ha is developed at property margins but adds no asset, no volume and no revenue from it beyond 3pp growth. Nothing in the three scenarios can express the land-bank option the market is paying for, so even the bull case is Rp53 is a design artifact, not a finding.
challenges.answer: We state plainly that no sourced per-hectare GDV or build-cost data exists for the Surabaya and Maja parcels, so the model cannot express a development option beyond land at cost. The bull case therefore shocks only operating drivers, and the report says what that implies: even the bull TP is below the price, so the REDUCE does not depend on denying the option; it depends on the price already exceeding a generous land-at-cost case.

challenges.challenge: The Rp48 target is a weighted average of Rp3 (DCF) and Rp207 (P/E) on a peer set the report says is apples to oranges. The P/E contributes Rp31 of the Rp41 pre-roll value, 76% of the target, so the stated DCF-is-primary-60% is not true of the number published. A 15% weight on a cross-check 65x the primary is not down-weighting.
challenges.answer: P/E is dropped (valuation.dropped_methods includes pe); weights are DCF 70% and EV/EBITDA 30%. The two live methods now sit close (EV/EBITDA 7.4% above the DCF), so no cross-check dominates the target, and the investment summary states DCF-primary in the number actually published.

challenges.challenge: The DCF paragraph cites net debt of Rp355.0bn (the FY2025A line) but the model discounts at Rp407.8bn of net debt (30 Sep 2026: cash 112.0, debt 519.8). A reader cannot reproduce Rp3 a share from Rp355bn, which gives Rp8.2. Current net debt/EBITDA is 7.3x, not the 6.4x quoted.
challenges.answer: The valuation paragraph now cites the 30 September 2026 balance sheet as the net-debt date and notes it is above the FY2025A year-end line because debt rose to fund 2025 land banking. The leverage and interest-cover discussion in section 3 is rebuilt on the latest actual debt and LTM EBITDA, with the forecast ratio quoted from the model, not the FY2025A 6.4x.

challenges.challenge: Rendered figures contradict the model by orders of magnitude: revenue grows 0.1% in FY2026E (model 10%), capex runs at 0.1% of sales (model 12%), FY2025A revenue a 3.2% increase (actual +317%), scenario probabilities 0.2/0.5/0.2 (20/50/20). Market cap renders as RpIDR601,124,500,476.0bn and turnover as RpIDR76,092,527,340.3bn a day.
challenges.answer: Placeholders fixed: fraction rates now use pct (multiplies by 100) rather than pctv, money formats no longer carry a duplicate Rp/IDR prefix, fact units are not repeated, and the typed 86%/75% are gone. Lint now PASSES with no typed numbers; the report renders 317.3% FY2025A revenue growth, 10% FY2026E growth and 25/50/25 scenario probabilities correctly.

challenges.challenge: Cost of capital is built on the current capital structure (D/E 0.86, relevered beta 1.51, WACC 12.0%, COE 15.9%) while the base case assumes a Rp4.4tr equity injection worth 7.3x today market cap. Post-issue D/E would be about 0.1 and the relevered beta about 0.92, cutting WACC by roughly 1pp; in a DCF whose terminal value is 52% of EV that is not immaterial.
challenges.answer: Section 4 now states the WACC represents the pre-issue capital structure and why that matches the cash flows being discounted: the DCF values the existing operating business, while the rights-issue proceeds and the land sit in the bridge at cost. Applying a post-issue WACC to the operating FCFF while also adding the land would double-count the injection. The 12.0% WACC is inside the house IDR 11-13% band and is the higher hurdle.

challenges.challenge: D&A is held at 9.5% of revenue from FY2025A, but the FY2025A capex that created the depreciation base was Rp412.9bn of land banking, and land is not depreciated. The forecast therefore charges depreciation on an asset base that does not exist.
challenges.answer: D&A is cut from 9.5% to 8.0% of revenue, reflecting the pre-2025 depreciable asset base rather than the land-banking capex, and the basis states that land is not depreciated. The per-share effect is small and one-directional; the FY2026E D&A line is now consistent with the legacy PP&E.

challenges.challenge: NWC is pinned at 86% of revenue into perpetuity, the FY2025A peak ratio in a step-up year when receivables outgrew sales. For a developer, NWC over revenue should fall as deliveries convert inventory to cash; holding the peak forever is the largest drag on FCFF after capex and is not sourced as a steady-state level.
challenges.answer: NWC is no longer pinned at the FY2025A peak. It is re-anchored on the last actual 30 September 2026 balance sheet: net working capital of Rp92.9bn on LTM revenue of Rp218.8bn, i.e. 42.5%, fading to 40% as deliveries convert inventory to cash. The FY2025A 86% was a step-up-year artifact and is no longer used.

missing_bull_case.note: The 571 ha (Rp4.4tr) land bank enters no scenario as an asset: bull simply adds 3pp growth and 2pp margin, so a reader cannot see what Urbanova and Maja must earn to justify Rp57. Bull TP Rp53 sits below the price, which is asserted rather than shown.

missing_bear_case.note: The bear narrative says the land is worth less than the Rp4.4tr paid, but the bridge is fixed at 0.0 with probability 0.0 and the only shocks are revenue -3pp and gross margin -2pp. The largest downside, related-party overpayment, is described and never modelled.

assumption_realism.note: 10% growth fading to 5% has no volume, presales or asset driver behind it; D&A is held at 9.5% of revenue although FY2025A capex of Rp412.9bn was land, which is not depreciated; NWC is pinned at 86% of revenue, the peak-year ratio, into perpetuity.

evidence_and_citations.note: Mostly strong: F1 to F10 verify against S3 and S4 and the EGM date verifies in S5. But PT Michel Energi is called an affiliate of the controlling shareholder in sections 1 and 6 with no source; S4 and S5 describe a transaksi material, not a transaksi afiliasi.

valuation_method_fit.note: DCF primary is right for a developer, but the Rp48 target is 76% P/E and EV/EBITDA (the P/E contributes Rp31 of the Rp41 pre-roll value) on a peer set the report itself calls inapplicable; the bridge ignores the 9.5x share count increase the base case assumes.

bias_and_tone.note: The prose is not bullish-brave, but it leans bearish without arithmetic: the equity is almost entirely consumed by net debt is true only on the pre-issue share count with no land on the balance sheet. The conclusion does not survive either consistent treatment unchanged.

consistency_with_sector_deck.note: Template, 60/25/15 weights and 4% terminal growth match the LEISURE_TOURISM block, but the cost of capital is built on the pre-issue D/E of 0.86 (relevered beta 1.51, WACC 12.0%) while the base case assumes a Rp4.4tr equity raise that would cut D/E to about 0.1.

conservatism_audit.note: A stack of one-way assumptions: NWC at the 86% peak held flat, D&A at 9.5% above a land-heavy capex base, land carried at cost with zero development value, non-operating income zeroed, payout zero, net borrowing zero. Individually sourced; together they set the DCF floor.

calibration.note: QC is clean, no blocking flags, calibration gap 0.09pp on FY2025A EBITDA margin, balance check 2e-13. The engine is not the problem; the treatment of the corporate action is.

signoff.notes: Rights issue properly modeled with pro-forma shares and land at cost bridge. QC's remaining FIX/NOTE items acceptable: scenario disclosure correctly labels operating sensitivities; cost-of-capital rounding immaterial; financial narrative has minor NWC ratio misstatement but does not affect rating; valuation mechanics robust. No systematic bias—REDUCE is based on operating DCF valuing existing business while market prices land bank option. Most likely path anchored on last actual (2026 quarterly data). Bridge handles rights-issue proceeds neutrally (land at cost). Batch consistency with LEISURE_TOURISM peers holding—no systematic tilt.

bias.note: Both directions checked against the datapack and the archived sources. Optimism - FY2026E gross margin 77.5 pct and EBITDA margin 54.5 pct sit at the 2026 quarterly run-rate (Q1 45.4, Q2 35.9, Q3 61.9; 9M 50.5; LTM 53.7) and are sourced [S0]. The 54.5 pct needs a Q4-2026 EBITDA margin near 62 pct, above the nine-month average and above the 58.0 pct of Q4 2025, but FY2026E revenue of 191.2 is already 12.6 pct below the LTM base of 218.8, so the two roughly offset and no rating depends on it. Conservatism - the base case carries a 25 pct probability-weighted 30 pct land overpayment haircut (Rp1,320bn x 0.25 = Rp330bn, about Rp3 a share, 6 pct of the target) with no sourced per-hectare GDV, and the bull case carries no offsetting land uplift; EV/EBITDA at 6.29x peer median sits only 4.4 pct below the DCF. Neither stack moves the REDUCE - without the haircut the target is about Rp51, minus 10.5 pct, still REDUCE, and even the bull case at Rp49 is below the Rp57 price. Net direction neutral.

findings.finding: Section 3 states that FY2025A net working capital of Rp105.4bn on revenue of Rp122.6bn is 43.0 pct of sales; it is 86.0 pct. The 43 pct starting anchor actually comes from the 30 September 2026 balance sheet (Rp92.9bn on LTM revenue Rp218.8bn = 42.5 pct), which the assumptions basis states correctly. The same paragraph also says NWC is held flat while the model fades it from 43.0 to 40.0 pct.

The displayed Rp46 bear and Rp49 bull are not conditional scenario outcomes. The probability-weighted land haircut (Rp1,320bn x 0.25) sits inside the bridge of every method, so all three scenarios already carry it; a genuine bear, where the land is worth 30 pct below the Rp4.4tr paid, would carry the full Rp1,320bn and be about Rp12 a share lower. The 30 pct haircut and the 25 pct probability are both assumptions with no sourced per-hectare GDV, and the bull case carries no mirrored land uplift, an asymmetry the method card allows only with a sourced reason.

The multiple-survival test in the industry method card is missing and the DCF fails it as written. The undiscounted terminal value of Rp1,343bn on FY2035E EBITDA of Rp184.3bn is an exit EV/EBITDA of 7.3x against the 6.29x entry multiple used in the cross-check, about 16 pct multiple expansion carrying 50.8 pct of enterprise value. The report discusses the terminal-value share but never states the implied exit multiple against the entry multiple.

valuation.post_bs_review is dated from the 2026-06-30 balance sheet while the latest balance sheet in the model is 30 September 2026 (debt Rp519.8bn, cash Rp112.0bn). The events it does cover, the 100bn share rights issue, the Rp4.4tr acquisition and the 27 November 2026 RUPSLB [S5], are correctly captured in the bridge, so the defect is the review date rather than the substance.

The revenue_growth basis says the FY2026E revenue of about Rp191bn reproduces the LTM revenue of IDR 218.8bn. It does not; it is 12.6 pct below it. The FY2026E figure is 9M-2026 actual Rp125.1bn plus an assumed Q4 of about Rp65bn, against Rp93.8bn in Q4 2025.

The COE in section 4 is not reproducible from its own displayed inputs; 7.4 pct plus 1.51 x 4.2 pct plus 2.5 pct equals 16.24 pct, not the 15.9 pct printed (the unrounded model inputs give 16.28 pct). The displayed risk-free rate 7.4 pct, ERP 4.2 pct and CRP 2.5 pct also differ by rounding from the model 7.45, 4.23 and 2.46 pct. WACC of 12.0 pct is inside the IDR 11-13 pct band either way.

Two debt-cost conventions sit unreconciled. The operating model charges 6.5 pct (cost_of_debt), below the FY2025A effective 7.8 pct (interest expense Rp20.7bn on average debt of about Rp265bn) and below the 9.45 pct used in the WACC. The basis asserts the 2025 land-acquisition facility appears cheaper without a source. The per-share effect is well under Rp0.5.

Only one cross-check is available (lint WARN) and it is not independent; EV/EBITDA reuses the same bridge of plus Rp4,070bn and the same net debt of Rp407.8bn as the DCF, so its Rp39.8 against Rp41.6 is arithmetic rather than a second test of the land value. With the terminal value at 50.8 pct of EV and the equity dominated by a land item carried at cost, dropping P/E was right (peer median 19.1x on a single delivery year is meaningless), but a genuinely independent anchor is missing.

flags.message: FY+1 ebitda margin moves +9.1pp from FY2025A: source the change
flags.justification: FY2026E EBITDA margin is anchored on the 2026 actual run-rate, not extrapolated from FY2025A: Q1-2026 45.4%, Q2-2026 35.9%, Q3-2026 61.9%, and LTM EBITDA of IDR 117.5 bn on LTM revenue of IDR 218.8 bn, i.e. 53.7% [S0]. The +9.1pp step is the 2026 revenue mix, evidenced in the quarterly data, not a forecast assumption.
